title: How competing onboarding checklists can get in the way of activation: a Scribe breakdown

Product Led Growth Product Design User Experience SaaS Product Management How competing onboarding checklists can get in the way of activation: a Scribe breakdown Riya Jawandhiya 6 min read · Just now -- Listen Share TL;DR The problem: Home shows two checklists that end in different places. The change: replace them with one path , install → capture → review. The measure: the share of eligible accounts that mark a first guide ready within seven days. What path to take? Should I become a pro user of Scribe, or should I complete my profile? Press enter or click to view image in full size On Home, the launch checklist has three steps: install the extension, create a guide, share it. Installation is complete, creation is available, and sharing comes after creation. Right beside it, the profile checklist has five tasks: install, pin, capture, share, invite teammates. Press enter or click to view image in full size At a glance they look like two views of the same job. They aren’t, because their endpoints differ. Pinning helps someone find the extension again. Capturing produces a guide. Sharing distributes it. Inviting teammates brings other people into the workspace. Each action has a reason to exist, but finishing one doesn’t require finishing the rest. Take someone documenting a process for their own future use . The guide is useful without a single invitation, yet the profile checklist still tells them there is work left. Press enter or click to view image in full size One the day on publishing, I checked scribe release a new home. It reduces clutter but the question still remains. A checklist is a claim about what the product thinks the job is. When two sit side by side, the product makes two claims, and the person has to guess which one counts. The risk is that finishing the account starts to feel like part of finishing the guide. I can see the competing definitions on screen, but I can’t see whether they actually delay anyone. Most other surfaces in the walkthrough were opened manually, and I don’t know what triggers the announcement, so none of it shows forced interruptions. Press enter or click to view image in full size I’m not reinventing the wheel. I’m taking things from what they have given and just optimizing it based on what I feel should be the goal for a one-time user, because I feel the invitation and the referral works only in the case of when they truly believe that this has solved a problem of theirs. That leaves a narrower question: should inviting teammates count toward first-session completion for someone making a private guide? Capture gives progress something to point at Once capture begins, numbered steps appear beside the work, with pause, delete and finish controls close by. The output is a private generated guide with a title, summary, screenshots, numbered instructions, duration, and Edit and Share actions. Here, progress has something to point to . The person can read what Scribe produced and decide what needs attention. That is a stronger basis for onboarding than account completeness, and it demands a harder definition of value. A generated guide is not a verified guide. The screens can’t tell me whether the steps are accurate, whether something important is missing, or whether a colleague could follow them. Opening the result proves even less. This is the part I find most useful. A tool that generates the work shifts the user’s job from creating to checking . Onboarding should land on that new job, not the old one. So for the first guide, the useful finish line is: review the steps, correct them where needed, and decide the guide is ready to use . If the guide is meant for someone else, the next proof belongs to the recipient . Can they complete the process without asking the creator to explain it again? An invitation gains a purpose when there is something worth inviting someone to use. Can we unify the checklists to attain all biz. goals? (I understand that money is required for a business to run, and as a product designer, you need to think on product side at that point as well. So you get higher conversions. Eventually, that is the only thing that is going to make your company successful. But how do you do that in a better experience?) I’d test one change on Home: replace both checklists with a single path , install → capture → review. Invitation stays available but stops counting as required first-session progress. After review, Share remains the next action for guides meant for someone else. It just doesn’t define done for a private guide. Home can’t tell a private guide from a shared one. One way to settle that: ask who this guide is for once, when capture starts, and let the answer set the finish line. Press enter or click to view image in full size The way of positioning it as who is this guide for is very different from share it with your friends, or invite your teammates because this way you question in a way that what is making it useful for them. The hypothesis in one sentence: a single path will raise the share of eligible accounts that mark a first guide ready within seven days, compared with today’s two checklists. The test has three parts. Who: randomize accounts that reach Home before creating a first guide, and report Skip arrivals separately. Primary measure: accounts that mark a first guide ready within seven days, divided by all eligible accounts in each version. Guardrails: invites sent per account, and abandonment.
